questions.q:
You are writing a summary of the benefits of a school garden. Which two of these sentences from Text B contain ideas you should include?

A. Ten years ago, the patch of land behind Hillside Primary School was a car park for delivery vans.
B. Surplus vegetables are given to a local food bank.
C. Slugs destroyed the first lettuce crop.
D. Children who struggle to sit still at a desk often concentrate well when their hands are busy in the soil.

Write the two letters. [2]
questions.tip: Background (A) and problems (C) are not benefits — always check each idea against the exact focus. Marking: If more than two letters are given, award 0 for any incorrect letter included (max 1).

questions.q:
Rewrite this sentence from Text B in your own words, as concisely as possible, so that it could be used in a summary:

“Measuring the growth of bean plants turns mathematics into something real.” [2]
ms: Meaning kept: the garden makes maths practical / relevant / shows how it is used in real life (1)
Own words and concise: key words changed (not ‘turns mathematics into something real’), example of bean plants generalised or removed (1)
questions.tip: Generalise the example (bean plants) and keep only the point it illustrates.

questions.q:
Text B – Growing more than vegetables (paragraphs 4 and 5)

There are quieter benefits as well. Working in small groups, pupils learn to share tools and take turns, and the head teacher believes playground arguments have fallen since the garden opened. Some anxious children say the garden is the place they feel calmest in school.
The garden also reaches beyond the school gates. Retired neighbours volunteer on Saturday mornings, passing on skills and forming friendships with families they would otherwise never have met. Surplus vegetables are given to a local food bank.

List four separate benefits of the garden from these paragraphs, in note form and in your own words. [4]
ms: Teaches cooperation / sharing / social skills (1)
Fewer arguments / better behaviour at break time (1)
Calms anxious pupils / improves well-being (1)
Older local people share their knowledge/skills (1)
Creates friendships / links between the community and families (1)
Extra food helps people in need / donated to the food bank (1)
questions.model:
• teaches pupils to cooperate
• fewer break-time quarrels
• calms anxious children
• older neighbours share skills and make friends with families
(Also: spare produce helps people in need.)
questions.tip: One idea per note; don’t combine two ideas in one bullet if you want them both credited.

questions.q:
A student began a summary of the benefits of the school garden like this:

“The school garden is great and I think every school should have one. Pupils who grow carrots and peas are far more willing to taste them. Slugs ate the lettuces. Mr Patel the caretaker jokes that he is an unpaid farmer.”

Identify four weaknesses in this extract. [4]
ms: Includes personal opinion/comment (“great”, “I think every school should have one”) — a summary should be objective (1)
Lifts/copies the wording of the text (“far more willing to taste them”) instead of using own words (1)
Includes an irrelevant point — the slugs are a problem, not a benefit (1)
Includes unnecessary anecdote/detail — Mr Patel’s joke adds no benefit (1)
Uses specific examples (carrots and peas) instead of generalising (vegetables) (1)
Wastes words — only one relevant idea in about 40 words / not concise (1)
questions.model:
1. It begins with the student’s own opinion, which does not belong in a summary.
2. The sentence about tasting vegetables is copied from the text, not in the student’s own words.
3. The slugs are a problem, not a benefit, so the point is irrelevant.
4. Mr Patel’s joke is an anecdote with no benefit in it, so it wastes words.
questions.tip: Opinion, lifting, irrelevance and anecdotes are the four most common summary faults.

questions.q:
Combine these three ideas from Text B into ONE sentence of no more than 30 words, in your own words, suitable for a summary:

• “Pupils who grow carrots and peas are far more willing to taste them.”
• “The school kitchen now serves salads made with the garden’s own produce.”
• “Parents report that children ask for vegetables at home.” [5]
ms: Idea 1: pupils more willing to try vegetables (1)
Idea 2: school meals use food grown in the garden (1)
Idea 3: children want/eat more vegetables at home too (1)
Own words throughout — no lifted phrases such as ‘far more willing to taste’ or ‘the garden’s own produce’; examples generalised (1)
One fluent, grammatical sentence of 30 words or fewer, with ideas logically linked (1)
questions.model: Growing food has made pupils keener to try vegetables, both at school, where meals now include the garden’s harvest, and at home. (22 words)
questions.tip: Use linking structures (‘both … and’, ‘where’, ‘which’) to fit several ideas into one concise sentence.

questions.q:
Read Text B, then answer the question.

Text B – Growing more than vegetables

Ten years ago, the patch of land behind Hillside Primary School was a car park for delivery vans. Today it is a garden of raised beds, fruit trees and a small pond, and teachers say it has changed far more than the view from the staffroom.
The most obvious change is in what children eat. Pupils who grow carrots and peas are far more willing to taste them, and the school kitchen now serves salads made with the garden’s own produce. Parents report that children ask for vegetables at home – something many never expected to hear.
Teachers have found the garden useful in lessons, too. Measuring the growth of bean plants turns mathematics into something real, and the pond has become an outdoor science laboratory. Children who struggle to sit still at a desk often concentrate well when their hands are busy in the soil.
There are quieter benefits as well. Working in small groups, pupils learn to share tools and take turns, and the head teacher believes playground arguments have fallen since the garden opened. Some anxious children say the garden is the place they feel calmest in school.
The garden also reaches beyond the school gates. Retired neighbours volunteer on Saturday mornings, passing on skills and forming friendships with families they would otherwise never have met. Surplus vegetables are given to a local food bank.
Not everything has been easy. Slugs destroyed the first lettuce crop, and the garden needs watering throughout the summer holidays, when the building is closed. The caretaker, Mr Patel, jokes that he has become an unpaid farmer.

According to Text B, what are the benefits of the school garden?
You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible.
Your summary should not be more than 120 words.
Up to 10 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 5 marks for the quality of your writing. [15]
ms: Indicative content (any relevant, clearly expressed idea is credited):
1. Pupils more willing to try/eat vegetables
2. School meals use fresh produce from the garden
3. Children eat/ask for vegetables at home — healthier habits spread to families
4. Makes maths practical/relevant
5. Provides an outdoor space for science lessons
6. Helps restless children concentrate/learn
7. Teaches cooperation/sharing/turn-taking
8. Fewer arguments / better behaviour at break time
9. Calms anxious children / improves well-being
10. Involves older local people, who share their skills
11. Builds friendships between the community and families
12. Spare food helps people in need (food bank)
13. Turned a car park into green space / improved the school environment
Not relevant: slugs, summer watering, Mr Patel’s joke (problems/anecdote)

levels.d: Demonstrates a thorough understanding of the text; selects a wide range of relevant ideas (about 11+), clearly focused on the benefits.
Good understanding; selects a range of relevant ideas (about 8–10); little irrelevance.
Some understanding; selects several relevant ideas (about 6–7), possibly with some irrelevance or repetition.
Limited selection of relevant ideas; may include problems, anecdotes or copied material that obscures understanding.
Concise, well organised and fluent; ideas grouped and linked; consistently own words; within 120 words.
Mostly clear and organised; mostly own words with some lifting; may be slightly wordy.
List-like, heavily copied, poorly organised or far over the limit; may include comment or opinion.

questions.model: The garden has made pupils more willing to try vegetables, both at school, where meals now include its fresh produce, and at home. It also improves learning: it makes mathematics practical, provides an outdoor space for science and helps restless children concentrate. Working together there teaches pupils to share and cooperate, which seems to have reduced conflict at break times, and it gives anxious children somewhere calm. Beyond the school, it connects families with older local people, who pass on their skills and form new friendships, while spare food is donated to people in need. Finally, it has replaced a car park with green space. (105 words)
questions.tip: Group ideas (food, learning, well-being, community) and link them — that earns the writing marks.
